summary: Outlines a set of goals for new IPv6 site-multihoming architectures, where a site connects through more than one provider. It admits the goals are ambitious and may conflict, so a solution may satisfy only some. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A site with two internet providers wants to keep working if one fails. This memo lists what a good solution should do, while admitting not all wishes can be met.

subtitle: Design goals for networks connected through multiple internet providers.

tldr.problem: As IPv6 deployment grows, many sites will connect through multiple internet providers for redundancy and load sharing, but the IPv4 approach to this causes the routing table to grow too large.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC sets out a list of goals and requirements that a good IPv6 multihoming solution must satisfy, balancing simplicity, scalability, redundancy, and transparency to applications.
tldr.outcome: This is a requirements document, not a solution. Later RFCs built multihoming solutions—most notably SHIM6—aiming to meet these goals.

today: RFC 3582 remains an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. The most prominent attempt to solve these goals was SHIM6 (RFC 5533), though SHIM6 was never widely deployed. The core challenge—scaling multihoming without bloating the routing table—remains a research topic in IPv6 deployments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Site-multihoming means a single organization connects to the internet through more than one Internet Service Provider (ISP). As more organizations do this for redundancy and performance, the global routing table becomes dangerously large.

The RFC notes that IPv4 multihoming works by publishing each multihomed site's addresses separately into the routing table, even when those addresses overlap with larger provider blocks. This creates unnecessary routing table entries.

The authors argue that IPv6, still early in deployment in 2003, should solve this problem from the start by designing a multihoming approach that lets sites remain multihomed without bloating routers' routing tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers have to remember where every website is. If many sites connect through multiple providers, routers remember too many addresses and get slow.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines three main roles. A site is an organization running its own network and making its own routing decisions. A transit provider is a company that sells internet access and connects other sites to the internet. A multihomed site has contracts with more than one transit provider.

When a site changes from one provider to another, that is called re-homing. The goal is for re-homing to happen with minimal interruption to ongoing conversations between the site's computers and the rest of the internet.
sections.plainLanguage: A site is like a company's office. A transit provider is like an electricity company. Multihoming is having two electricity companies so if one cuts off power, the office keeps running.

sections.title: Requirements for a Good Solution
sections.content:
The RFC lists eight capabilities that IPv4 multihoming already provides, which any IPv6 solution should keep: Redundancy (switching to a backup provider when one fails), Load Sharing (spreading traffic across providers), Performance (avoiding congested paths between providers), Policy (choosing providers for business reasons, not just technical ones), Simplicity (not harder to operate than IPv4), Transport-Layer Survivability (ongoing conversations don't break during re-homing), DNS Compatibility (working with how domain names are looked up), and Packet Filtering (being able to block packets with fake source addresses).

The RFC adds eight additional requirements. Scalability is the big one: a solution must allow orders of magnitude more multihomed sites without growing the routing table beyond what routers can handle. The solution must also not require major changes to routers or hosts, must handle interactions between hosts and routing systems securely, allow site operators to manage it, and avoid requiring cooperation between competing providers.
sections.plainLanguage: A good solution lets a site switch providers without breaking phone calls, doesn't make routers too heavy, and lets the site control how it sends traffic.

sections.title: Security Constraints
sections.content: Multihoming must not create new security weaknesses. The RFC points to two requirements: multihomed sites must be no more vulnerable to attacks than traditional sites, and the changes to routing needed for multihoming must not make non-multihomed sites easier to attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Using multiple providers shouldn't make a site easier to break into than a normal site.
